after.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$ exists.

In order for ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to exist, the left- and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

* Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}({e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x) \\  & ={e}^{1}+{1}^{2}+1 \\  & =e+2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

* Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=x+a.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(x+a) \\  & =1+a.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) \\ 1+a & =e+2 \\ a & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$ exists.

In order for ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to exist, the left- and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

* Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}({e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x) \\  & ={e}^{1}+{1}^{2}+1 \\  & =e+2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

* Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=x+a.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(x+a) \\  & =1+a.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) \\ 1+a & =e+2 \\ a & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $f(x),$ defined as follows:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x, & x\le 1 \\ x+a, & 1<x<3 \\ {x}^{2}-2x, & x\ge 3\end{aligned}
$$

Current part:

It is known that $f$ is continuous at $x=1.$ Find the value of $a.$

content.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$ exists.

In order for ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to exist, the left- and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

* Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}({e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x) \\  & ={e}^{1}+{1}^{2}+1 \\  & =e+2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

* Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=x+a.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(x+a) \\  & =1+a.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) \\ 1+a & =e+2 \\ a & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: On [4,7], f(x)=x²−2x. For n equal rectangles, the width is 3/n and the left endpoints are 4+3k/n for k=0,…,n−1. Each summand is the function value at a left endpoint multiplied by 3/n.

after.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x$ and the $x$-axis between $x=4$ and $x=7$ as the following definite integral:

$$
A={\int }_{4}^{7}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

This definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

	

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

In the definite integral above, the function is $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x,$ the lower bound is $a=4,$ and the upper bound is $b=7.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{7-4}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{7}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(4+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(4+\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{(4+\frac{3k}{n})}^{2}-2(4+\frac{3k}{n})]\cdot \frac{3}{n}.\end{aligned}

We want to express the area $A$ between $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x$ and the $x$-axis between $x=4$ and $x=7$ as the following definite integral:

$$
A={\int }_{4}^{7}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

This definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

	

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

In the definite integral above, the function is $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x,$ the lower bound is $a=4,$ and the upper bound is $b=7.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{7-4}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{7}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(4+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(4+\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{(4+\frac{3k}{n})}^{2}-2(4+\frac{3k}{n})]\cdot \frac{3}{n}.\end{aligned}

content.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x$ and the $x$-axis between $x=4$ and $x=7$ as the following definite integral:

$$
A={\int }_{4}^{7}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

This definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

	

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

In the definite integral above, the function is $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x,$ the lower bound is $a=4,$ and the upper bound is $b=7.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{7-4}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{7}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(4+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(4+\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{(4+\frac{3k}{n})}^{2}-2(4+\frac{3k}{n})]\cdot \frac{3}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$
